Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The उपनिषद्स् are a treasure-होउसे of spiritual wisdom. One of the more ancient उपनिषद्स् assigned to the period 2000 B. C. but not classed among the major ones is the Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad (also known as the Maitrī Upaniṣad) since it was originally taught by the sage Maitri and belongs to the Maitrāyaṇīyaśākhā (śākhā = recension) of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
The longer version as available now has seven prapāṭhakas or chapters and 73 mantras, both in prose and in poetry.
The Upaniṣad starts with the story of the king Bṛhadratha who renounced his kingdom and did severe austerities to realise the आत्मन्. A sage, Śākāyanya by name, came to his place whereupon the king fell at his feet and begged him to teach about the आत्मन्. Being pleased with his earnest entreaties, the sage started teaching him.
The वालखिल्यस्, the tiny sages, had got this wisdom from Kratu प्रजापति and the sage मैत्री taught the same to Śākāyanya.
The various and varied teachings of this Upaniṣad may be summarised as follows:
The आत्मन्, though encased in the body, is really free. This आत्मन् is full of many blessed qualities and enlivens the body with चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. The whole च्रेअतिओन् has emerged out of प्रजापति (the Lord of creatures). In this body there are two selves, the जीव (individual Self) and the पर (Supreme Self). The पर or ब्रह्मन् is attained by विद्या (knowledge), तपस् (austerity) and cintā (meditation). There are several gods like अग्नि (fire), वायु (air), आदित्य (sun), and the trimūrtis (Brahmā, विष्णु and रुद्र); but they are all manifestations of the same ब्रह्मन्.
The other topics dealt with are: प्रणव or ओङ्कार; the three worlds bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and suvaḥ; gist of the गायत्री मन्त्र; taking ड़ोओद् compared to a sacrifice; importance of time as a cosmic element; some methods of योग which are similar to the ones described in the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.); description of the मुक्तपुरुष or the liberated person.
Mentioning of the kings of the Solar and the Lunar dynasties, a knowledge of अस्त्रोनोम्य्, familiarity with the Sāṅkhyan metaphysics and an indication about the existence of the fine-arts like drawing and dramaturgy—these are some of the specialities noted in this Upaniṣad.

Maitreyī
------------------------------------------
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.4 and 4.5) has immortalised मैत्रेयी by depicting her as a woman of high spiritual aspirations who cared more for मोक्ष or emancipation than for worldly wealth.
She was the first wife of the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य, the second being कात्यायनी.
When याज्ञवल्क्य decided to renounce worldly life and take to the monastic life, he called both of them and announced his decision, not only about his leaving the होउसे as a recluse but also about the dividing of his property between them. Though कात्यायनी was happy with getting her share of the property, मैत्रेयी was more interested in that for the sake of which her husband was renouncing the world. On hearing that he was doing so for attaining मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence, she begged him to teach the same to her also, rejecting the other offer of worldly wealth and possessions.
Then follows a long discourse by याज्ञवल्क्य on the existence and attainment of the आत्मन्, for whose sake only, people love one another.
These two sections of the Upaniṣad—2.4 and 4.5—are known as Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa.
See also YĀJÑAVALKYA.

Maitrāyaṇīya Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
The Saṁhitā part of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda is said to have had 85 शाखास् or recensions. However, only four are available now, out of which the Maitrāya-ṇīya Saṁhitā is the second. It is a mixture of prose and verses. It has 2144 mantras out of which 1701 have been borrowed from the Ṛgveda itself. Some of its mantras find a place in the Kāṭhaka and Taittirīya Saṁhitās also.
This Saṁhitā has four kāṇḍas or books, each divided into prapāṭhakas or subsections.
The following are the contents:
Prathama or Ādima Kāṇḍa: It has eleven prapāṭhakas. Some वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् like दर्शपूर्णमास, चातुर्मास्य and वाजपेय are described here.
Dvitīya or Madhyama Kāṇḍa: This contains thirteen prapāṭhakas dealing with some kāmyeṣṭis (desire-motivated sacrifices), राजसूय and Agniciti (rite of piling the fire-altar).
Tṛtīya or Upari Kāṇḍa: This comprises sixteen prapāṭhakas. Sacrifices like the अश्वमेध and Sautrāmaṇi are described here.
Caturtha or Khila Kāṇḍa: Containing fourteen prapāṭhakas, this section deals with many important and necessary accessories and rites connected with the sacrifices described in the other three sections.

maitrāvaruṇa
(‘belonging to मित्र and वरुण’)
------------------------------------------
A Vedic sacrifice needs four principal priests: होतृ, अध्वर्यु, उद्गातृ and ब्रह्मन्.
Each one of these can have three assistants, taking the total number to sixteen, which is the maximum.
Maitrāvaruṇa is an assistant priest attached to the होतृ, the first of the four major priests (who are sometimes called ‘mahartvij’). His duty is to recite the hymns to the Vedic deities मित्र and वरुण at the prātassavana or morning pressing of the सोम juice. He also gives instructions, sometimes, to other priests.
He is associated with पशुबन्ध sacrifices—sacrifices involving the immolation of paśus or animals—also.

maitrī
(‘friendship’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedic sages while recognising the existing natural divisions of the society also prescribed some sāmanya dharmas or common virtues to be practised by all the human beings irrespective of their आश्रम or वर्ण, thus contributing to greater peace and harmony in the society. Some of these are: अहिṁसा (non-violence), सत्य (truth), अस्तेय (non-stealing), kṣānti (forbearance) and so on.
One such common virtue is मैत्री or an attitude of friendship towards all (vide Brahmapurāṇa 114.16-18).
Patañjali (200 B. C.) in his monumental work, the Yogasūtras considers the cultivation of मैत्री or an attitude of friendship towards those who are happy will help in attaining greater control over one’s मिन्द् (vide sūtra 1.33).

Maitreya
(‘son of Mitrā’)
------------------------------------------
One of the well-known sages mentioned in the epics and the पुराणस्, he was the son of Kauṣārava (or Tuṣārava) and Mitrā. On hearing that the Pāṇḍavas were banished to the forest, he advised धृतराष्ट्र (the blind king and the ड़थेर् of the Kauravas) to make peace with them. दुर्योधन (the eldest of the Kauravas) patted his own thighs out of arrogance which enraged the sage who cursed him to die due to broken thighs.
The Viṣṇupurāṇa was taught to मैत्रेय by the sage पराशर (father of the famous व्यास).
The sage बक-दाल्भ्य (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.12.1) was also known as मैत्रेय.
Maitreya is prominently mentioned in the Bhāgavata also.
